passages.title: Climate Change: Causes and Effects
passages.subtitle: How rising global temperatures are reshaping weather, coastlines, and farming
paragraphs: Over the past century, the average temperature of the Earth has risen faster than at any other time in modern history. Scientists call this long-term warming trend global warming. The main cause is human activity—especially burning coal, oil, and gas for electricity, factories, and transport. These activities release huge amounts of carbon emissions and other greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.

Normally, greenhouse gases act like a thin blanket that keeps our planet warm enough for life. However, when too many of these gases build up in the air, they trap extra heat from the sun. As a result, oceans and land surfaces become warmer every decade, changing natural climate patterns around the world.

One of the clearest effects of a hotter planet is extreme weather. Many regions now experience longer heatwaves, stronger tropical storms, and sudden heavy floods. In dry areas such as parts of Australia and California, hotter summers dry out forests and grass, leading to dangerous wildfires that destroy homes and wildlife habitats.

Higher temperatures are also causing melting ice caps in Greenland and Antarctica. As massive sheets of ice turn into water and flow into the oceans, coastal communities face rising sea levels. Low-lying island nations and major port cities already report more frequent street flooding during high tides, forcing local councils to spend billions building higher sea walls.

Farming and daily life are heavily affected too. Unpredictable rainfall and sudden droughts can cause serious crop failure, leaving farmers with little rice, wheat, or fruit to sell. When harvests shrink, food prices rise in supermarkets, hurting ordinary families. Meanwhile, some scientists and planners argue that while we must cut emissions, societies also need to learn how to live with climate change by planting heat-resistant crops and designing cooler, greener buildings.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 2

passages.title: Economic Growth or Environmental Protection?
passages.subtitle: Can countries lift citizens out of poverty without destroying natural ecosystems?
paragraphs: A For many governments around the world, achieving strong economic growth is the number-one goal. Opening new factories, expanding trade, and building highways create millions of jobs and help lift people out of poverty. Over the past fifty years, rapid industrial development has given hundreds of millions of families access to electricity, clean housing, and better schools.

B However, traditional growth has come at a heavy environmental cost. Dr. Samuel Mensah, an environmental scientist in Ghana, warns that unmanaged factories and mining operations quickly deplete resources such as forests, minerals, and clean rivers. 'When rivers become polluted and farm soil loses its quality, local families suffer from health problems and lower crop yields,' he says. 'A rich economy cannot survive on a damaged planet.'

C On the other hand, developing countries often feel it is unfair to ask them to slow down. Maria Lopez, an economist in Peru, points out that wealthy nations grew rich in the past by burning coal and cutting down forests without strict green laws. 'Poorer regions still need affordable power and basic roads for their citizens,' she argues. 'If strict environmental rules close local factories too quickly, unemployment and hunger will rise.'

D Because both sides have valid points, international leaders now promote sustainable development—growing the economy in a way that meets today's needs without harming future generations. The key goal is to strike a balance between creating jobs and keeping air, water, and forests healthy.

E One promising path is building a green economy. Kenji Takahashi, a clean-tech adviser in Japan, explains that protecting nature can actually create new wealth. 'Investing in solar farms, electric buses, and modern recycling plants creates thousands of skilled local jobs while cutting air pollution,' he notes. In his view, green industries offer a smarter way to grow than old smoky factories.

F Global support is also essential. Dr. Sarah Al-Noor, a policy researcher in Jordan, believes wealthy countries should share clean technology and offer low-interest loans to developing nations. 'If rich nations help fund clean energy projects abroad, developing countries can lift citizens out of poverty without repeating the polluting mistakes of the past,' she concludes.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 3
passages.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.
passages.title: Climate Change: Risk or Opportunity for Business?
passages.subtitle: How companies adapt to climate damage while investing in green technology
paragraphs: 1 In the past, many business leaders treated climate change as a distant problem for scientists and politicians. Today, however, changing weather is directly affecting company profits around the world. From family farms to global factories, firms are discovering that climate change brings both serious financial risks and surprising new business opportunities.

2 Several major industries already face heavy losses. Agriculture suffers directly when floods or droughts ruin coffee, cocoa, and grain harvests. The tourism industry is also vulnerable: ski resorts receive less natural snow each winter, while coastal hotels struggle with severe storms and beach erosion. Meanwhile, insurance companies have to pay out record sums every year to repair buildings damaged by extreme weather.

3 Even companies far from storms can run into trouble through their supply chain—the network of factories, farms, and ships that deliver parts and goods. If a major flood shuts down a factory in one country, carmakers or clothing brands on the other side of the world may face costly delays. In addition, more governments are introducing a carbon tax, charging companies money for the greenhouse gases they release.

4 Yet climate change is not only bad news for business. As countries try to cut emissions, the renewable industry is growing at record speed. Firms that design green technology—such as solar panels, battery storage, and smart energy-saving appliances—are attracting billions of dollars from banks and private funds eager to invest in clean growth.

5 Ordinary shoppers are also pushing markets in a greener direction. Surveys show that younger customers increasingly prefer eco-friendly products, including recycled clothing, refillable packaging, and plant-based snacks. Companies that listen to these buyers and reduce waste often build stronger brand loyalty while saving money on electricity and raw materials.

6 In short, climate change is separating forward-looking businesses from those stuck in the past. Firms that ignore environmental warnings risk losing money from damaged supplies, higher carbon taxes, and unhappy customers. By contrast, businesses that adapt to new conditions early and invest in clean ideas are likely to become the market leaders of the next decade.
